intro: Open a book. Is it a story? Or is it true? A frog in a red hat is a story. A photo of a real frog is true. Both are good. But you read them in different ways.

In a story, look for the characters, the setting and the events. Find the problem and the fix. Then retell it in order. In a true book, look for the topic, the headings, the labels and the captions. Find the facts.
By the end of this unit, you will be able to open any book and say what kind it is, tell what it is about, and find what you want to know inside it.
bigQuestion: How do you read a story, and how do you read a true book?

timeline.t: Look at the cover. Read the title. Find the author and the illustrator.
Is it a story or a true book? Look for a talking animal or a photo of a real thing.
In a story, find the characters. In a true book, find the topic.
Find the setting: where and when the story happens.
Spot the problem. Watch for what the character wants.
In a true book, use the table of contents and headings to find the part you need.
Read the pictures, the labels and the captions. They hold facts too.
Find the solution. See how the problem gets fixed.
Close the book. Tell it in order: first, next, then, last.
Ask who, what, where, when and why. Answer each one from the book.
Say what the story teaches, or what fact you learned from the true book.

words.d: a person or animal that the story is about
where and when a story happens
something that is wrong or hard for a character
how the problem gets fixed
to tell a story again in your own words, in order
something that is true and can be checked
big words at the top of a part that tell what it is about
words under a picture that tell what it shows

test.q: The hare and the tortoise are the ones the tale is about. What are they?
test.why: Characters are the people or animals a story is about.

test.q: A story happens in a park on a snowy day. What is that?
test.why: The setting is where and when a story happens.
The solution is the way the problem is solved.

test.q: Which words help you retell a story in order?
test.why: Order words keep the events in line when you retell.

test.q: Which question word asks for a reason?
A book has a frog that talks and wears a hat. What kind of book is it?
test.why: Real frogs do not talk. The author made it up, so it is a story.

test.q: Frogs lay eggs in water. What is that?
test.why: A fact is true and can be checked. You find facts in true books.

test.q: Where do you look to find what page Tadpoles is on?
test.why: The table of contents lists each part and its page number.

test.q: A line points to a frog's eye and the word says eye. What is that?
test.why: A label names one part of a picture.

test.q: Who writes the words in a book?
test.why: The author writes the words. The illustrator makes the pictures.

write.prompt: Pick one book you know. Is it a story book or a true book? Say which one. Then give two things from the book that show you are right.
tips: Start with your claim: This book is a story book, or This book is a true book.
Give proof. Does an animal talk? Are there photos of real things? Are there headings or captions?
Say why your proof shows it. Talking animals mean made up. Facts and photos mean true.
Think about the other side. Could someone say it is the other kind? Say why they are wrong.

title: Stories and True Books

chapters.title: Who, Where, What Happens
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you know what a story is really about?

story.title: The Slow One and the Fast One
story.kicker: A very old tale. A hare who is fast. A tortoise who is slow. Guess who wins.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz reads to her class in Chicago. It is a very old tale. A hare can run fast. A tortoise walks slow. The hare laughs at the tortoise. So the tortoise says, "Let us race." The hare says yes.
The race starts. The hare zooms off. He is far ahead. He looks back. The tortoise is a tiny dot. The hare says, "I have time." He lies down under a tree. He falls asleep.
The tortoise does not stop. Step. Step. Step. She walks past the sleeping hare. She walks to the line. The hare wakes up. He runs as fast as he can. Too late. The tortoise wins.
The class talks about it. Jae says, "The hare was fast, but he took a nap." Ruby says, "The tortoise never quit." Ms. Ortiz smiles. "Now you know what the story is about," she says.
story.think: The hare is faster. Why did the tortoise win the race?

lessons.title: Who Is in the Story
lessons.mainIdea: The characters are the people or animals a story is about.
reading: Think about the race. A hare. A tortoise. They are the ones in the story. They talk. They run. They do things. We call them the *characters*.
A character can be a person. A character can be an animal. A character can even be a talking cup! If it does things in the story, it is a character.
When you open a book, ask, "Who is this about?" Look at the pictures. Look at the names. Find the characters first. Then the story makes sense.

words.d: a person or animal that the story is about

look.title: The Lost Mitten
look.text: Look at this story. A boy named Sam drops his red mitten in the snow. A small dog finds it. The dog runs after Sam. The dog drops the mitten at his feet. Sam laughs and says thank you.
look.prompt: Who are the characters in this story?

check.q: What is a character?
choices: A person or animal in the story
The last page of the book
check.why: A character is who the story is about. The hare and the tortoise are characters.

check.q: Can an animal be a character?
choices: Yes, if it does things in the story
Only if it is a dog
check.why: A character can be a person, an animal or even a talking cup. It just has to do things in the story.

check.q: What is a good first question when you open a book?
check.why: Finding the characters first helps the story make sense.

lessons.title: Where and When It Happens
lessons.mainIdea: The setting is where and when a story happens.
reading: The hare and the tortoise race on a road. It is a sunny day. There is a tree. The hare naps under it. The road, the day, the tree. That is the *setting*.
The setting is where a story happens. It is also when. A story can happen in a city. It can happen on the moon. It can happen at night or long ago.
The setting changes the story. Snow means cold. A dark forest means scary. Look at the pictures to find the setting. Ask, "Where are they? When is it?"

words.d: where and when a story happens

look.title: Same Story, New Place
look.text: Picture a girl looking for her cat. Now put her in a quiet farm at noon. Now put her in a big city at night, with buses and lights. Same girl. Same cat. But the story feels very different.
look.prompt: Which setting makes the story feel scarier? Why?

check.q: What is the setting of a story?
check.why: The setting is the place and the time of the story.

check.q: Where does the race in the tale happen?
choices: On a road on a sunny day
In a boat on the sea
check.why: The hare and the tortoise race on a road. It is sunny, and there is a tree.

check.q: A story is set in a dark forest. How will it feel?
check.why: The setting changes how a story feels. A dark forest feels scary.

lessons.title: What Happens
lessons.mainIdea: Events are the things that happen in a story, one after another.
reading: The race starts. The hare runs ahead. The hare takes a nap. The tortoise walks past. The tortoise wins. Each thing that happens is an *event*.
Events come in order. First one thing. Then the next. Then the next. If you mix them up, the story breaks. The hare cannot nap before the race starts!
When you read, keep a list in your head. What happened first? What happened next? What happened last? Those are the events.

words.d: one thing that happens in a story

look.title: Three Things Happen
look.text: Picture this. A girl plants a seed in a cup. She waters it every day. A tiny green leaf pokes up. Three things happened. Each one is an event. Each one comes after the last one.
look.prompt: What was the first event? What was the last one?

check.q: What is an event?
choices: One thing that happens in a story
check.why: An event is one thing that happens. The hare taking a nap is an event.

check.q: What happens after the hare takes a nap?
choices: The hare laughs at the tortoise
check.why: While the hare sleeps, the tortoise keeps walking and passes him.

check.q: Why do the events need to stay in order?
choices: Mixing them up breaks the story
check.why: Events happen one after another. The hare cannot nap before the race starts.

lessons.title: What a Character Wants
lessons.mainIdea: Every character wants something, and that want moves the story.
reading: The hare wants to win. The tortoise wants to win too. She also wants the hare to stop laughing at her. A *want* is what a character is trying to get.
Ask, "What does this character want?" Then watch what they do. The tortoise wants to win. So she keeps walking. She never stops. Her want tells you why she does it.
Every story has a want. A dog wants a bone. A girl wants a friend. A boy wants to fly a kite. The want makes the story go.

words.d: the thing a character is trying to get

look.title: Leo and the Kite
look.text: Leo runs across the park with a kite. It drags on the grass. He runs again. It flops. He runs into the wind this time. The kite lifts up. Leo shouts. Watch what Leo does again and again. It tells you what he wants.
look.prompt: What does Leo want? How do you know?

check.q: What does the tortoise want?
check.why: The tortoise wants to win. That is why she keeps walking.

check.q: How can you tell what a character wants?
choices: Watch what the character keeps doing
check.why: What a character does again and again shows what they want.

check.q: Why does the tortoise never stop walking?
check.why: Her want to win tells you why she keeps going.

lessons.title: How a Character Feels
lessons.mainIdea: Words and pictures show how a character feels.
reading: The hare laughs at the tortoise. He feels proud. He feels sure he will win. At the end, he loses. Now he feels surprised. Maybe a little sad. These are his *feelings*.
A book does not always say the feeling. It shows it. A big smile means happy. Tears mean sad. Stomping feet mean mad. Look at the face in the picture. Look at what the character says.
Feelings can change. The hare felt proud at the start. He felt shocked at the end. Ask, "How does the character feel now?" Ask it again later.

words.d: what a character feels inside, like happy, sad or mad

look.title: Look at Her Face
look.text: Picture a page in a book. A girl stands by a broken bike. Her mouth is turned down. Her arms hang low. She looks at the ground. The words only say, "Mia stood by her bike." But you know how she feels.
look.prompt: How does Mia feel? What in the picture tells you?

check.q: How does the hare feel at the start of the race?
check.why: The hare laughs at the tortoise. He is sure he will win.

check.q: A character stomps her feet. How does she likely feel?
check.why: Stomping feet is a way a book shows that a character is mad.

check.q: Can a character's feelings change in a story?
check.why: The hare felt proud at the start and shocked at the end. Feelings change.

lessons.title: The Problem and the Fix
lessons.mainIdea: Most stories have a problem, and the story shows how it gets solved.
reading: The tortoise has a *problem*. The hare is faster. How can she win? A problem is something that is wrong or hard for a character.
The story shows the fix. The tortoise keeps going. The hare naps. She passes him. The problem is solved. That is the *solution*. A solution is how the problem gets fixed.
Find the problem in every story. Then find the solution. Sam lost his mitten. The dog found it. Problem, then solution. Most stories work this way.

words.d: something that is wrong or hard for a character
how the problem gets fixed

look.title: The Stuck Ball
look.text: Look at the yard. A ball is stuck up in a tree. Two kids look up at it. They cannot reach. Then one kid gets a broom. She pokes the ball. It drops. Both kids cheer.
look.prompt: What was the problem? What was the solution?

check.q: What is the tortoise's problem?
choices: The hare is faster than she is
She does not like the road
check.why: The hare is faster. The tortoise must find a way to win anyway.

check.q: What is a solution?
choices: The way a problem gets fixed
check.why: The solution is how the problem is solved. The tortoise keeps going and wins.

check.q: The ball is stuck in a tree. The girl pokes it with a broom. What is that?
check.why: The stuck ball is the problem. Poking it down is the solution.

lessons.title: Tell It in Order
lessons.mainIdea: To retell a story, say the events in order: first, next, then, last.
reading: Close the book. Now tell the story. First, the hare laughs at the tortoise. Next, they race. Then the hare naps. Last, the tortoise wins. That is a *retelling*.
Use order words. First. Next. Then. Last. They keep the events in line. Say who the characters are. Say where it happens. Say the problem and the fix.
The pictures can help you. Flip through them. Each picture shows an event. Point to a picture. Say what happens. Move to the next one.

words.d: to tell a story again in your own words, in order

look.title: Pictures in a Picture Book
look.prompt: Use the pictures to retell the story. Which event comes third?

check.q: What are the order words?
check.why: First, next, then and last keep the events in order when you retell.

check.q: What happens first in the tale?
choices: The hare laughs at the tortoise
check.why: The story starts with the hare laughing. That is why the tortoise asks to race.

check.q: How can pictures help you retell?
check.why: Each picture shows one event. Point to each one and say what happens.

lessons.title: Ask Good Questions
lessons.mainIdea: Who, what, where, when and why questions help you understand a story.
reading: Who raced? The hare and the tortoise. Where? On a road. When? On a sunny day. What happened? The tortoise won. Why? The hare took a nap. These are the *question words*.
Who asks about the characters. Where and when ask about the setting. What asks about the events. Why asks for the reason. Every story can answer all five.
Ask them before you read. Ask them while you read. Ask them after. If you can answer all five, you understand the story.

words.d: who, what, where, when and why

look.title: Five Questions, One Story
look.text: Here is a tiny story. On Monday morning, Ana found a lost puppy at the park. She took it home because it was cold. Who? Ana. Where? The park. When? Monday morning. What? She found a puppy. Why did she take it home? It was cold.
look.prompt: Which question word asks about the setting?

check.q: Which question word asks about the characters?
check.why: Who asks about the people or animals in the story.

check.q: Why did the tortoise win the race?
check.why: The hare stopped and slept. The tortoise kept going and passed him.

check.q: Which question asks for a reason?
check.why: Why asks for the reason something happened.

lessons.title: Two Tales, One Lesson
lessons.mainIdea: Two versions of a tale can differ, but each story teaches a lesson.
reading: Ms. Ortiz reads a second book. This time the race is in a city. The hare rides a scooter. The tortoise walks. The hare stops for ice cream. The tortoise still wins.
Two books can tell the same tale. That is a *version*. The setting changed. The hare's nap became ice cream. But the characters, the problem and the ending stayed the same.
Both books teach the same *lesson*. Keep going and do not quit. A lesson is what the story wants you to learn. Ask, "What did the character learn?" That is the lesson.

words.d: one way of telling a tale that can be told many ways
what a story wants you to learn

look.title: Same Race, Two Books
look.text: Book one: a road, a tree, a nap. Book two: a city, a scooter, an ice cream stop. In both, the hare is faster. In both, the hare stops. In both, the slow one wins. Two versions. One lesson.
look.prompt: What is the same in both books? What is different?

check.q: What changed in the second version?
choices: The setting and the hare's stop
check.why: The city, the scooter and the ice cream are new. The tortoise still wins.

check.q: What is the lesson of the tale?
choices: Keep going and do not quit
check.why: The tortoise wins because she never stops. That is what the story wants you to learn.

check.q: How do you find the lesson of a story?
check.why: The lesson is what the character learns. Ask that question and you will find it.

review.q: Who are the characters in the old tale?
review.why: Characters are who the story is about. The hare and the tortoise race.

review.q: The race happens on a road on a sunny day. What is that?
review.why: The setting is where and when the story happens.
The hare is faster. She solves it by never stopping.

review.q: Which words help you retell in order?
review.why: Order words keep the events in line when you retell.

review.q: The hare laughs at the tortoise. How does he feel?
review.why: Laughing at the tortoise shows the hare feels proud and sure he will win.

review.q: The second book has a city and a scooter. What stayed the same?
review.why: Two versions can change the setting. Both teach: keep going and do not quit.

chapters.title: Story Books and True Books
chapters.bigQuestion: How can you tell if a book is made up or true, and how do you find facts in it?

story.title: Two Frogs on One Table
story.kicker: Two books about frogs. In one, the frog talks. In the other, it does not. Which one is true?
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz puts two books on the table. Both have a frog on the cover. Both are green. Jae picks up the first one. A frog named Pip wears a red hat. Pip says, "I lost my hat!" Pip hops to the pond to find it.

Ruby picks up the second book. There is a photo of a real frog. The words say, "A frog lays its eggs in water." There is a small picture of the eggs. Under it, more words say, "Frog eggs look like jelly."
"Frogs do not talk," says Ruby. "And they do not wear hats." Jae looks at his book again. "This one is made up," he says. "But it is a good story." Ruby holds up hers. "This one is true."
Ms. Ortiz nods. "One book is a story. One book is a true book. Both are about frogs. But you read them in different ways." Today the class will learn how.
story.think: How did Ruby know that her frog book was the true one?

lessons.title: Some Books Are Made Up
lessons.mainIdea: A story book is made up by the author, even if it feels real.
reading: Pip the frog wears a hat. Pip talks. Pip hops to the pond to find his hat. None of this really happened. The author *made it up*. That makes it a story book.
A story book has characters. It has a problem. It has events in order. It can have talking animals. It can have magic. It does not have to be real.
Made up does not mean bad. Stories are fun. Stories teach lessons. But you do not use a story to learn facts. Pip cannot teach you what real frogs eat.

words.d: not real; something the author thought up

look.title: The Hat Hunt
look.text: Look at a page from Pip's book. Pip stands by the pond. A fish pokes its head out of the water. The fish says, "Is this your hat?" It holds up a red hat with its fin. Pip claps his hands.
look.prompt: What on this page tells you the book is made up?

check.q: What does made up mean?
choices: Not real; the author thought it up
check.why: Made up means the author thought it up. Pip the frog is not real.

check.q: Which one shows a book is a story book?
choices: It has a photo of a real frog
The frog talks and wears a hat
It has a list of facts
check.why: Real frogs do not talk or wear hats. A talking frog means the book is made up.

check.q: Can a story book teach you what real frogs eat?
choices: Yes, if the frog is green
No, you need a true book for facts
check.why: Stories are fun and teach lessons, but facts come from true books.

lessons.title: Some Books Are True
lessons.mainIdea: A true book gives facts about real things.
reading: "A frog lays its eggs in water." That is a *fact*. It is true. Someone checked it. Ruby's book is full of facts. It is a *true book*.
A true book is about one thing. It might be frogs. It might be trucks. It might be the moon. It tells you facts about that thing. The pictures show real things.
You read a true book to learn. You can start at any page. You can read just the part you need. You do not have to read it in order like a story.

words.d: something that is true and can be checked
a book that gives facts about real things

look.title: Two Pages, Side by Side
look.text: On the left, a drawing of Pip in his red hat, waving. On the right, a photo of a real green frog on a lily pad. Under the photo it says, "A frog can jump 20 times its body length."
look.prompt: Which page is from the true book? How can you tell?

check.q: What is a fact?
choices: A thing that is true and can be checked
A thing the author made up
check.why: A fact is true. Someone can check it. Frogs really do lay eggs in water.

check.q: How do you read a true book?
choices: You can start at the part you need
check.why: A true book is for learning. You can read just the part you need.

check.q: What kind of pictures are in a true book?
check.why: The pictures in a true book show real things, like a photo of a real frog.

sections.title: The Parts of a True Book

lessons.title: Headings Tell You What Is Next
lessons.mainIdea: A heading is a big title on a page that tells what that part is about.
reading: Ruby turns a page. Big dark words sit at the top: What Frogs Eat. Under them, smaller words tell about flies and bugs. The big words are a *heading*.
A heading is like a sign. It tells you what the next part is about. Frog Eggs. Where Frogs Live. What Frogs Eat. Each heading starts a new part.
Use the headings to find things. Want to know what frogs eat? Look for that heading. Skip the rest. Headings save you time.

words.d: big words at the top of a part that tell what it is about

look.title: Find the Right Part
look.text: You want to know where frogs live. You flip through the true book. You see these headings, one on each page: Frog Eggs. Tadpoles. Where Frogs Live. What Frogs Eat. Frog Sounds.
look.prompt: Which heading should you stop at? Why?

check.q: What is a heading?
choices: Big words that tell what a part is about
check.why: A heading is the big title at the top of a part. It tells what comes next.

check.q: You want to know what frogs eat. What do you look for?
check.why: Headings help you find the part you need. Look for the one about eating.

check.q: Why do headings save time?
choices: You can skip parts you do not need
check.why: Headings tell you what each part is about, so you can go right to the part you want.

lessons.title: Labels and Captions
lessons.mainIdea: Labels name the parts of a picture, and captions tell what the picture shows.
reading: Ruby's book has a photo of a frog. A line points to its back leg. The word by the line says leg. Another line points to the eye. It says eye. Those words are *labels*.
Under the photo there is one short sentence. "This tree frog lives in a rain forest." That sentence is a *caption*. A caption tells you what the picture shows.
Labels name parts. Captions tell about the whole picture. Read both. Sometimes the caption has a fact that is not in the big words.

words.d: a word that names one part of a picture
words under a picture that tell what it shows

look.title: Read the Whole Page
look.text: Picture a photo of a frog egg. A line points to a black dot in the egg. The word says tadpole. Under the photo it says, "A tadpole grows inside the egg for about a week."
look.prompt: Which words are the label? Which words are the caption?

check.q: A line points to the frog's leg. The word says leg. What is that?
check.why: A label names one part of a picture.

check.q: What does a caption do?
choices: Tells what the whole picture shows
check.why: A caption is the words under a picture. It tells what the picture shows.

check.q: Why should you read the captions?
choices: They may have a fact that is not in the big words
They tell you the book is over
check.why: Captions can hold extra facts. Reading them helps you learn more.

lessons.title: The Table of Contents
lessons.mainIdea: The table of contents lists the parts of a book and their page numbers.
reading: Open the true book to the first pages. There is a list. Frog Eggs, page 4. Tadpoles, page 6. Where Frogs Live, page 10. This list is the *table of contents*.
The table of contents shows every part of the book. Next to each part is a page number. Find the part you want. Turn to that page.
Story books do not need one. You read them in order. But true books do. The table of contents helps you jump right to the facts you need.

words.d: a list at the front of a book that shows the parts and their pages

look.title: A Table of Contents
look.prompt: You want to read about tadpoles. What page do you turn to?

check.q: Where is the table of contents?
choices: At the front of the book
check.why: The table of contents is on the first pages of a true book.

check.q: What is next to each part in the table of contents?
check.why: Each part has a page number so you can turn right to it.

check.q: Why do true books need a table of contents?
choices: So you can jump to the part you need
check.why: You do not have to read a true book in order. The list helps you find the right part.

lessons.title: Topic and Details
lessons.mainIdea: A true book has one main topic, and the details are the facts about it.
reading: What is Ruby's whole book about? Frogs. That is the *topic*. The topic is the one big thing the book is about. The title often tells you the topic.
Now look inside. Frogs lay eggs in water. Frogs eat bugs. Frogs have long back legs. Each fact is a *detail*. Details tell you more about the topic.
Think of a tree. The topic is the trunk. The details are the branches. Every branch is part of the tree. Every detail is about the topic.

words.d: the one big thing a true book is about
a fact that tells more about the topic

look.title: One Big Thing
look.text: A book is called All About Trucks. Inside it says: Trucks carry heavy loads. Some trucks have ten wheels. A fire truck carries water and a ladder. A dump truck can tip its bed.
look.prompt: What is the topic of this book? Name one detail.

check.q: What is the topic of Ruby's book?
check.why: The whole book is about frogs. Frogs are the topic.

check.q: Which one is a detail about frogs?
check.why: Frogs eat bugs is a fact that tells more about the topic, frogs.

check.q: What often tells you the topic?
check.why: A true book's title often names its topic, like All About Trucks.

lessons.title: Ask, Then Find the Answer
lessons.mainIdea: Ask a question first, then use the book's parts to find the answer.
reading: Jae has a *question*. "Do frogs have teeth?" He does not know. So he picks up the true book. A question is what you want to find out.
He looks at the table of contents. He finds What Frogs Eat, page 14. He turns to it. He reads the heading. He reads the words. He reads the caption. There it is.
The book says most frogs have tiny teeth on top. They do not chew with them. They swallow food whole. Jae found his answer. Ask, look, read, find.

words.d: something you want to find out

look.title: Ruby's Question
look.text: Ruby wants to know how big a frog egg is. She looks at the table of contents. She sees Frog Eggs, page 4. She turns to page 4. Under a photo, the caption says, "Each egg is about the size of a pea."
look.prompt: What steps did Ruby take to find her answer?

check.q: What is the first step in finding a fact?
check.why: First you ask what you want to know. Then you look for it.

check.q: Where did Jae look to find the right page?
check.why: The table of contents told him What Frogs Eat was on page 14.

check.q: Where did Ruby find her answer?
choices: In the caption under a photo
check.why: The caption under the egg photo said each egg is about the size of a pea.

lessons.title: Two Books, One Animal
lessons.mainIdea: Two books can be about the same animal but tell it in different ways.
reading: Both books are about frogs. Pip's book is a story. Ruby's book is true. Same animal. Different kind of book. We can *compare* them. To compare is to look at what is the same and different.
What is the same? Both have a green frog. Both show a pond. What is different? Pip talks. The real frog does not. Pip's book has a problem. Ruby's book has facts.
Two true books can be compared too. One might have more photos. One might tell more about eggs. Read both. Then you know more than one book can tell you.

lessons.title: The Author and the Illustrator
lessons.mainIdea: The author writes the words, and the illustrator makes the pictures.
reading: Look at the cover of Pip's book. Two names are on it. One person wrote the words. That is the *author*. One person drew Pip. That is the *illustrator*.
Sometimes one person does both. Sometimes it is two people. The author thinks up the story or finds the facts. The illustrator draws or takes the photos.
In a true book, the pictures matter a lot. The illustrator shows real things. A photo of a real frog helps you see the facts.
